units: the clogging of the access roads comes from motorists setting off at the same moment
each driver believes that pressing on alone is in his own interest
traffic specialists see sensible choices whose sum produces the opposite effect
a first solution is to spread the start of work across the morning
staggering departures thins out the crowding at the busiest moment
a second measure gives one lane over to cars carrying several occupants
that reserved lane rewards the sharing of a vehicle
applying both measures together improves the speed and the punctuality of public transport
the main obstacle is the lack of coordination between separate decision makers
text: Why do the roads into a town centre seize up morning after morning? The cause is a dull one: nearly every driver sets off at the same moment. Each of them reckons that pressing ahead alone will save time, and the queue lengthens for everybody. Traffic engineers describe a heap of reasonable decisions adding up to an absurd result. Two remedies come round again and again. The first is to spread the leaving hour: employers stagger the start of shifts, and the busiest moment thins out across a wider stretch of the morning. The second hands one lane over to vehicles carrying more than a single occupant, which rewards those who share a journey. Where both have been tried at once, average speeds climb again and the buses keep to their timetable. So the obstacle is not a technical one. It lies in getting bodies that decide separately to decide together.

units: a delivery cyclist had ridden the same machine for seven years
his old bicycle was heavy and rattled over uneven ground
the bicycle lent by the workshop was slimmer and quicker on the flat
he expected to be won over but felt uneasy at first
the old machine forgave clumsy riding
the borrowed one reacted harshly under braking
after a week he decided that each machine had an advantage of its own
he gave the trial model back
he simply replaced his braking parts
text: Seven years on one bicycle had made the courier stubborn, and it took some persuading before he agreed to try another. His old frame was a weight, the wide bars pushed his shoulders open, and the rear mudguard rattled over every rut. The machine lent by the workshop was its opposite: slender tubing, more spokes, deep rims that carried him along the flat with no effort at all. He had expected delight. What he felt, for the first hour, was unease. The old bike forgave a clumsy line; the borrowed one punished the smallest wobble. The pads bit so hard that he nearly went over the bars. By the end of the week he had his verdict, and it was even: the light machine won on speed, the old one on trust. He gave the trial bike back and changed nothing but his brakes, which struck him as the better bargain.

units: an hour set aside for checks is advised before a long journey
the front screen has to be cleaned inside as well as outside
the mirrors are set once you are sitting where you drive
the pressure in the tyres is taken while they are not hot
the state of the brakes is seen through the opening in the wheel
the fluid levels under the bonnet have to be topped up
a level that drops quickly points to a loss from the circuit
the heaviest luggage goes at the bottom of the load space
writing the checks down makes later departures easier
text: Before a long drive, give yourself an hour and work through it in blocks. You will save yourself a sulk at the roadside. Seeing out comes first: clean the windscreen on both faces, check the wipers leave no smear, then sit where you actually drive and set each mirror from there. Wheels next: take the tyre pressures while they are cold, look along the tread for uneven wear, and peer through the spokes at the pads. Fluids after that: lift the bonnet and top up the washer bottle, the coolant and the oil, and if a level drops quickly, that is a leak and not thirst. Loading last: heavy things at the bottom of the boot, nothing loose on the back shelf, and strap down whatever sticks out. Write what you checked in a small notebook. Next time you set off you will start calm instead of guessing.

units: the first train came out of the depot before sunrise
people living nearby watched the departure from behind barriers
the freshly laid rail link serves the warehouse area and the station
the works had begun four years earlier
shifting the underground pipes was the costliest stage
laying the power cables was held up by a shortage of parts
the runs without passengers brought a track connection fault to light
the opening to the public was put off twice
traders in the area grew angry at those delays
text: The first tram rolled out of the depot before the sun was up, watched by people from the surrounding streets pressed against the barriers. The freshly laid line joins the warehouse district to the station, closing a scheme begun four years ago. The opening months went on shifting pipes and ducts beneath the ground, work nobody would ever see and by far the dearest part of the whole undertaking. Rails followed, then the overhead power cables, held up by a shortage of parts. Empty running brought to light a fault in the points at the depot mouth, put right within three weeks. The start of services to the public slipped twice, which wore down the patience of shopkeepers cut off from their custom. The engineer in charge now insists that the promised frequency will be met within weeks.

units: a narrow strip of grass runs along the roadway
the manoeuvres of passing vehicles have damaged the edge of the road
two parallel grooves have worn into that border
rain sits in those hollows instead of reaching the ditch
the trapped water softens the ground and breaks up the edge of the surface
vehicles squeezing over to the side deepen the wear
stakes driven in by those living along it are flattened by wide trailers
the low light of evening makes those deformations easier to see
this old road carries a far heavier traffic than the one first intended
text: A band of cropped grass runs beside the narrow road, and it is the grass that gives the story away. Years of awkward passing have let wheels bite into the verge, whose surface has dropped away into two long parallel grooves. Rain gathers in them instead of running off to the ditch; it soaks downwards, softens what lies beneath, and the edge of the surfacing splits away in flakes. Every vehicle that squeezes over widens the trough a little further. Those who live along the road drove in stakes to mark the limit, but the stakes lean now, torn loose by trailers built too wide. When evening comes, the low light picks out each hollow and the lane looks stitched with dark scars. From that ruined margin alone you can read the load carried by a track laid out for carts and handed over to lorries.

units: the wearing out of a road depends above all on the weight borne by each axle
the damage rises far more steeply than the mass, following a power law
one laden lorry harms the upper layer as much as a very great number of cars
engineers know this mechanism
the rules on financial contribution take no account of this mechanism
the sum asked of hauliers depends mainly on the dimensions declared
a first correction would be to charge for the load measured under each axle
sensors set into the road surface would make that measurement possible
a second correction would be to spread the goods over more axles
text: Nothing wrecks a road surface like the weight riding on a single axle. The damage does not rise in step with the load; it climbs as a steep power of it, so that one laden lorry chews through the upper layer as thoroughly as many thousands of cars. Engineers in the highways offices have known this for a long while. The rules that decide who pays take no notice of it: what a haulier is charged turns mostly on the size declared for the vehicle. Two corrections follow. Charge for the load actually pressing on each axle, read off sensors buried in the surfacing, and not for a tonnage written on a form. Then reward operators who spread the same freight across extra axles, something trailer builders have long known how to do. A network priced by the damage it takes would cost less to keep up than one priced by guesswork.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager of the depot first worked as a driver
she drove on services that ran at night
she holds that the two roles differ in almost everything
at the wheel the attention goes to things happening at once
in management the effects of a decision show up long afterwards
as a driver she judged her success by arriving on time
as a manager she judges it by the steadiness of every route together
she has kept the habit of listening to the sounds a vehicle makes
she values what a driver reports more than readings from instruments
text: The woman who runs the bus depot began her working life at the wheel, on the services that ran through the night. Two jobs that look neighbouring, she says, turn out to share almost nothing. Driving, your world ends at the windscreen: a signal, someone stepping off the kerb, a door that will not shut. From behind a desk the view stretches across seasons, and an order given one week shows its effect months afterwards. As a driver she measured herself by reaching the terminus on time; running the depot, she measures the steadiness of every route at once. One habit from the old job stayed with her, and she rates it highly: listening to the bodywork. A groan from an axle, reported by a driver, is worth more to her than a screen full of readings. Her former workmates grumble only that she has grown strict about deadlines.

units: the appraisal deals with a shared bicycle service opened not long ago
the mechanical design of the machines is held to be sound
the parts that wear can be changed without special tools
such ease of repair is unusual for a fleet of this sort
the docking points are too tightly gathered in the central area
spaces grow scarce in the districts that lie higher up
a user going down early finds no space on the way back
the scale of charges favours short trips and punishes long hires
the adjustment of the saddle and the height of the bars are found comfortable
text: Three things are worth weighing up in the shared bicycle service that opened not long ago. The engineering comes first, and it earns respect: a heavy frame, reinforced rims, mudguards welded rather than bolted, brake pads you can reach without a special tool. Worn parts can be swapped out, which is rare enough on a fleet of this sort. The spread of docking points is the obvious weakness. Stands cluster in the middle and thin out as soon as the ground rises, so anyone who freewheels down at dawn comes back to find every slot taken. Charges are the third matter: short hops are cheap, long hires punished hard, which suits errands but discourages anyone riding for pleasure. One kind word on comfort, though. The saddle adjusts one-handed, and the bars sit high enough for a tender back.

units: the writer puts his message together while sitting in a train
the train follows a narrow valley
he left his starting point very early with an overloaded bag
the coach at the beginning of the journey suffered a puncture
the driver mended it while grumbling about the sloping verge
the passengers had to help shift the vehicle
that incident made him miss his rail connection
someone at a ticket window sent him on to a train stopping everywhere
he finds the experience worthwhile in the end despite the delay piling up
text: I am writing this from a carriage that is following a narrow valley, and I want to give it to you in order, because the day has earned it. I left at first light with a bag far too heavy and far too much faith in my connections. An hour out, the coach picked up a puncture; the driver got the jack out, grumbled at the verge for sloping, and had us all pushing. So I missed the train I was booked on, of course. At the next halt a woman at the ticket window put me on a service that stops everywhere, and I watched hamlets go by that I would never have looked at otherwise. Around midday I shared my lunch with a couple coming back from a house move. The delay piled up and I minded none of it. I will get in late, tired, with two notebooks full. Do not pity me. I think I came out ahead.

units: the question put is whether stops with few users should be closed
the specialist in planning holds that the question is badly framed
she puts the thin custom down to the spacing of the services
a service that comes rarely drives users away
the fall in custom then serves to justify further cuts in provision
she reckons that travel booked on demand can break that circle
she insists that booking be possible by voice call as much as through the internet
she stresses that a vehicle without passengers costs almost as much as a full one
she concludes that closing a stop treats the effect and strengthens the root of the trouble
text: Should stops that almost nobody uses be closed? The engineer in charge of planning answers that the question itself is put the wrong way round. Thin custom, she explains, follows from thin service: when vehicles come rarely, people give up waiting for them, and the emptier the stop looks, the easier it becomes to cut again. We ask whether booking a ride on demand breaks that loop. She believes it can, on one condition, that a journey may be ordered by telephone as readily as through a screen, or the scheme shuts out the very people it claims to serve. On cost, she points out that a vehicle running without a soul aboard costs nearly what a full one costs, while a small bus matched to real demand trims the bill. Closing a stop, she concludes, treats the symptom and feeds the root of the trouble.
